steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been broken for three days when Elias first saw the boy on the rocks.

He was carrying a bucket of seawater up the slick path, blue boots slipping, one mitten lost to the wind. The boy set the bucket at the base of the lighthouse, caught his breath, then looked up. The glass room at the top flashed once, white and cold.

Elias did not move from his chair.

The storm warning had come at dawn: a smudge of ink on the radio’s tiny screen, low pressure racing in from the west. Offshore, crab boats were already turning for harbor, their masts pricking holes in the gray horizon. Inside the lighthouse, the wind hummed in the stone as if the tower were an organ pipe.

He listened to it from his place beside the lantern room’s narrow window, a chipped mug cooling in his hands. Below, the town lay folded into the curve of the cove, roofs beaded with the last of last night’s rain. Above, the sky was no one color yet, just a gather of shades that promised more.

The boy was early.

Elias watched him fumble with the latch at the service door, the ridiculous red scarf the boy’s mother insisted on flapping like a distress flag. He counted the beats of his own heart until it had slowed, then he set the mug on the floor and went down.

His knees went first, always, on the spiral of stone steps—thirty-eight of them; he had counted too many times to forget—and they reminded him of each landing, each decade. The smell of oil and salt and old paint lived in the core of the lighthouse, and sometimes he imagined it had seeped into him, lining his lungs with a film of the place.

By the time he reached the bottom, the boy had given up on the latch and was simply banging on the door with the flat of his palm.

“Finn,” Elias said, opening it.

Finn skidded half into him, breathless and damp-cheeked. “It’s coming early,” he said, as if the storm belonged to them, as if it reported to no one else.

“So I’ve heard.” Elias looked past him at the restless sea. “You lost a mitten.”

Finn held up his bare hand as if surprised. “Oh. Gran’ll be cross.”

“She’ll be cross you’re here at all,” Elias said. “You know how she gets about weather.”

“Wouldn’t let me go to school,” Finn said proudly, as though this were a medal. “Said the road might wash out. So I brought you water.”

They both looked at the bucket. It was brimming, little waves lapping at its metal rim.

“You know the pump works,” Elias said. The old well behind the lighthouse was stubborn but not dead yet, and it did not require a boy to haul the sea.

Finn shrugged. “Salt water’s better for the tower. Da says so.”

“Your da,” Elias said, “used to lie whenever it suited him.”

Finn’s face tightened, the way it did whenever his father was mentioned. The boy had his father’s jaw and his mother’s eyes, and somehow the worst and best of both. It pained Elias to look at him sometimes, and he tried not to let it show.

“Bring it in anyway,” he said more gently. “The stone’ll drink it.”

Finn brightened. He heaved at the bucket, nearly lost his grip, and Elias caught the handle with two fingers, taking most of the weight. They carried it in together, boy and old man, leaving a trail of dark dots across the threshold.

“You hear from him?” Finn asked, as they set the bucket by the wall.

“Your da?” Elias shook his head. “Sea’s busy. He’ll write when he can.”

“He promised,” Finn said. “Last time. He promised he’d be back for the next big blow.”

“He promised a lot of things.” Elias straightened slowly, feeling the vertebrae stack and complain. “Tide doesn’t listen to promises either, but it comes all the same.”

Finn frowned at this, trying to wrestle it into sense. “You think he’s on a boat right now?”

“I think,” Elias said, “we’ve got a storm to prepare for.”

It was the safest answer. It left room for hope, which was the one thing Elias had never successfully taken away from anyone.

Finn followed him up the inner steps, swinging his bare hand along the rail. “Can I light it later?” he asked. “The lamp? You said when I was big enough.”

“You can barely carry a bucket,” Elias replied, but there was no bite to it. “We’ll see.”

He had expected to be alone in this tower for the rest of his working life. When they automated the light five years ago, the Bureau had sent a man in a clean shirt and spotless boots to explain the future. “Central control,” the man had said, tapping a glossy pamphlet that smelled of fresh ink. “No more need for round-the-clock staff. Sensors. Predictive maintenance.”

Elias had listened, watched the man’s mouth move, then signed the papers with a hand that did not tremble until afterwards. They cut power to the old Fresnel and installed a new assembly in its place—LED arrays stacked like teeth, capable of throwing coded pulses twenty miles into the black. The tower would blink and sweep, just as it always had, but no human needed to be present.

Except the town had not trusted this. Except the closest central office was two hundred miles inland. Except storms here could knock out any wire, any signal, any brand new, flawless future.

So in the end, they left Elias the keys.

“Call it redundancy,” the Bureau man had said, already thinking of other things. “Back-up. Temporary.”

Temporary had lasted five years so far.

On the third landing, Finn stopped to peer through the slit window at the cove below. “Mum’s washing’ll blow right off the line,” he pronounced.

“She should have taken it down when the warning came,” Elias said.

“She said if the wind wanted it, it could have it,” Finn replied. “Said she wasn’t going to dance to the weather anymore.” He glanced up. “Gran told her she was foolish.”

“Gran’s often right,” Elias said. “Even when she’s unpleasant about it.”

Finn snorted laughter, then clapped his bare hand over his mouth as if he’d let something dangerous escape.

At the lamp room door, Elias paused. The brass handle was worn to silk, the paint on the wood smoothed by decades of palms. His father’s, his own, a few others in between whose names he said to himself sometimes before sleep.

He saw Finn’s mittenless hand hover, wanting to touch, to belong to that line of hands.

“Go on,” Elias said. “Gently.”

Finn’s fingers brushed the handle as if it were the flank of a sleeping animal. “Feels warm,” he whispered.

“It remembers,” Elias said, and did not elaborate.

The lantern room, when they stepped in, was a ring of glass and light. Even with the lamp off, the day itself seemed brighter up here, the ocean all around pressing its colors against the panes. The new array sat in the center like a white metal heart, wiring neatly bundled, the old Fresnel lens packed and crated months ago, now nothing more than weight in a warehouse far from salt.

Elias missed it in a way that felt like missing a limb. The lens had sung when he cleaned it. It had bent light into a blade that could cut through rain. This new thing merely performed.

“Foghorn’s still broken,” Finn said, as if it were a personal insult.

“Yes,” Elias said. “I told them last week. They’ll say they’ll send someone after the storm.”

“They never do,” Finn said.

“They do,” Elias corrected. “Just not when we want them to.”

He moved around the array, checking the seals on the glass panes, listening for any whistle that would mean a bad fit. He ran a hand along the circuit box, felt the faint thrum that meant power was flowing.

“Help me with the shutters,” he said.

They folded down the inner steel covers halfway, practice against the worst winds. Finn grunted with the effort. The first fat drops of new rain hit the glass while they worked, each one a small, temporary star.

“You ever been out in one?” Finn asked suddenly. “A real storm, in a boat?”

“Yes.”

“Was it bad?”

Elias thought of black water, higher than roofs, of ropes like live snakes, of a man’s shout cut short as the sea took him. He thought of his own hands then, younger and bleeding, clinging to slick rail, and of the far-off wink of the very light he now tended, a promise and an order all at once.

“It was what it was,” he said.

“You were scared,” Finn said, pleased to have found chink in the myth of him.

“A sensible man’s always scared at sea,” Elias said. “Only fools are not. Your father”—he swallowed the rest—“knows that.”

Finn went quiet.

The radio crackled on the table by the door. The coast station’s voice cut through static, listing coordinates, wind directions, a litany of numbers that were comfort to some and gibberish to others.

“Winds increasing to sixty knots by midday,” the voice said. “Gale warning in effect. All vessels advised to seek safe harbor.”

Finn’s eyes went to the white blur on the horizon. “He’ll come in,” he said. “Da. He promised.”

Elias set a hand on the boy’s shoulder. It was as slight as a gull’s wing there. “Most do,” he said.

“And if he doesn’t?” Finn pressed.

“Then we’ll keep the light on,” Elias said. “So he knows where the rocks are. That’s our part.”

For an hour, they worked. Finn wiped down instruments with a care so fierce it was almost reverence. Elias checked fuel reserves for the backup generator, made sure the emergency batteries were topped. He spoke less than usual. The storm, crouching offshore, had its own presence in the room. It was a listener too.

By the time the north edge of it hit, the lighthouse was a drum. Wind struck its flank in turns and rolls, rattling the glass, booming in the stairwell. Rain came in sheets so thick the town disappeared behind it. Somewhere below, a loose shutter clapped like a mad hand until Finn ran down and bolted it fast.

“Feels like it’s angry,” he panted when he returned.

“It’s only wind and water,” Elias said. “They don’t care enough to be angry.”

But he thought of the first time he had tended this light alone, twenty-four and trembling with the responsibility. How he had stood in this very room in another storm and felt the tower sway, just perceptibly, under the assault, and believed for a moment that the sea had finally decided to reclaim its place.

“Mum’ll be scared,” Finn said, eyes tracking where he thought the town should be. “Gran pretends she’s not, but she is.”

“They’ve done this before,” Elias reminded him. “More times than you’ve seen winters.”

“Da says he’s not scared of anything.” Finn’s voice had gone soft.

“Then your da’s a liar,” Elias said. “Or a fool. Maybe both. You can love him and still know that.”

Finn bristled, then deflated. Outside, the gray thickened. The first flicker of power loss stuttered through the room: the overhead bulb dimmed, brightened, dimmed again.

“Generator,” Elias said. He moved to the panel, watching the red and green indicators. A moment later, the main line dropped entirely, and the pale hum of the array faltered.

The storm had taken the town.

The batteries caught the load without a hiccup. The array’s internal circuits lit up again, steady, though now it was the stored chemical patience of lead and acid doing the work.

Finn let out a breath he’d been holding.

“Told you,” Elias said quietly. “Redundancy.”

They stood together, watching the beam cut its slow, precise arc across the darkening sea. On, off, on, off. Index of a book written in waves.

“You know the pattern?” Elias asked.

Finn nodded. “Four seconds on, two off, four on, fourteen off. We learned it in school. Mrs. Cale made us write it out.” He hesitated. “She said we could see it all the way from the outer bank, if we were there.”

“You can,” Elias said. “I have.”

Finn turned to him with something like accusation. “You’ve been everywhere.”

“I’ve been enough places,” Elias said. “This one took me back.”

“Why’d you come back?” Finn asked.

Elias looked out at the line where sea and sky were negotiating the terms of today. “Because someone has to keep the light.”

“They could’ve left it to the machines,” Finn pointed out. “Like they wanted to.”

“They did,” Elias said. “But sometimes the machines fail. And sometimes a boy comes up the hill with a bucket of water, and someone needs to tell him when the wind’s going to turn.”

Finn seemed to weigh this, lips moving slightly, as if he were rearranging the words inside himself until they fit a place.

A burst of static from the radio made them both jump. Through the hiss, a voice, thinner now, pushing hard against distance and interference:

“—vessel Chanter—engine—drifting—requesting assistance—”

Finn went still.

“Chanter,” he whispered. “Da’s boat.”

The voice faded, snapped back, broken in half by the storm’s teeth.

“—six miles—east by southeast of—Point—taking on water—can’t—”

“Can you answer?” Finn asked, grabbing Elias’s sleeve. “Tell them we hear them?”

Elias was already at the set, thumb on the transmit key, though he knew what the answer would be. The tower had a receiver, but no transmitter worth the name. They could listen. They could not speak.

He pressed the key anyway, watched the little orange light, heard only the hollow click of his own attempt. The official line was that every boat now had satellite and redundancy upon redundancy. The official line said lighthouses were obsolete as anything but sentimental landmarks.

Elias stared at the radio as if will alone could reverse the last decade’s budget decisions.

Outside, the rain thickened again, and the sound came like a hand across the glass.

“Can’t we do anything?” Finn’s voice was high now, tight. “We’ve got to do something.”

Elias stepped to the glass, squinting through the spinning curtain. The beam swept, swept again. Somewhere beyond the reach of his eye, a boat that should have come in with the others was losing its fight.

He thought of the longshore rescue team, of their truck waiting in the station below, of the men and women now suiting up, judging their window between fury and impossibility. He thought of the old charts in the drawer that no one bothered with anymore, replaced by screens and satellites.

“Get your coat,” he said.

Finn blinked. “What? Where are we—”

“Get your coat,” Elias repeated. “And both mittens, if you can find the lost one on the way down.”

“But—Gran—”

“Gran will chain me to the wall herself when this is over,” Elias said. “And she’ll be right to. Go.”

Finn ran.

Alone in the lamp room, Elias went to the battered cabinet beneath the workbench. It held his personal relics now—things the Bureau hadn’t cared enough to catalog. A sextant, brass tarnished. A compass in a cracked leather case. A rolled chart, edges frayed. He took the chart out and spread it flat.

The shoals east by southeast of the point were a scatter of pet names and teeth. Devil’s Ridge. Mother’s Breath. Gull’s Table. He had sounded them himself once, in a smaller, softer storm. He knew where the channels ran.

The storm crawled its fingers up the glass, impatient.

By the time Finn returned, breathless, his scarf re-tied, both mittens miraculously present, Elias had the chart folded under his arm and his own coat on.

“You’re not going out there.” Finn panted.

“I am not leaving this tower,” Elias said. “But there’s something else we can do.”

He pushed past the boy and headed down the stairs. The familiar ache in his knees was drowned now by a different pounding.

At the second landing, Finn grabbed the rail. “If we’re not going out—”

“We’re changing the light,” Elias said.

“You said you can’t—we’re not supposed to—”

“The Bureau isn’t here,” Elias said thinly. “We are.”

In the service room below, he rummaged through another drawer until he found what he wanted: a battered logbook, pages soft as skin. Part of the old protocol, back when each keeper recorded not just weather and fuel and passing traffic, but any deviations in the signal. Warnings, messages, codes.

“You know semaphore?” he asked.

“Um.” Finn blinked. “Flag stuff? Mrs. Cale showed us once.”

“Forget flags.” Elias opened the log, ran his finger down a column of notations. “In the war, and after, when the radios were worse, we had a system. Changing the light’s pattern meant something. Two short flashes meant ‘harbor closed’. One long meant ‘submerged hazard’.” He stopped at a particularly underlined entry. “Alternating double and single—distress, friendly vessel. This one—” His finger tapped. “Rotating double-flash, long pause—direct to safe channel.”

“We can do that?” Finn whispered.

“We are not supposed to.” Elias closed the log with a thump. “But today we are.”

Back in the lamp room, he opened the control box for the array. Rows of tiny switches and a small, unfriendly screen blinked diagnostics at him. The Bureau man had shown him once, briefly, how to adjust the timing. “Not that you’ll ever need to, really,” the man had said, smiling, everything temporary.

Elias had taken notes anyway.

Now he input the code with fingers that did not feel old at all. Four-two-four-fourteen—that was the tower’s official signature, its name in light. He overrode it, heart thudding at the little warning icon that appeared: UNREGISTERED PATTERN.

“Sea doesn’t read icons,” he muttered, and committed the change.

The beam faltered for a breath, then resumed, now with a new rhythm: double-flash, double-flash, long dark, single-flash, longer dark. A heartbeat stutter, repeating.

Finn watched, eyes wide. “Will he know?” he asked, as if his father could read this from miles away.

“If he can see it, he’ll know something’s different,” Elias said. “If he remembers his training, he’ll know what it means. If he doesn’t—” He stopped. “We’re doing our part.”

Down in the town, if anyone was looking up through the sheets of rain, they might squint at the change, might wonder if the aging keeper was finally losing his mind. The Bureau
